Learning Objectives
Define fracture-related infection.
Describe the manner in which biofilm affects the management of fracture-related infection.
Apply the Cierny-Mader staging system for osteomyelitis.
Review treatment principles for fracture-related infection.
Epidemiology
Fracture-related infection (FRI) may occur in as many as 55% of patients with a fracture,
depending on the severity of bony and soft-tissue injury, fracture location, and patient factors.

Epidemiology
FRI may occur in as many as 55% of patients with a fracture, depending on risk factors,
such as fracture location, the nature of the bony or soft-tissue injury, patient factors, and
environment.1 The true incidence of FRI is unknown because the literature includes
various definitions of FRI.2
Etiology
FRI is inclusive of postoperative infection, infected nonunions, and osteomyelitis that occur
after fracture.
A distinction is made between acute (<6 weeks from fixation) or chronic (>6 weeks from
fixation) infections.
Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus,
Streptococcus, Enterococcus, and Pseudomonas.

Etiology
The term FRI is inclusive of postoperative infection, infected nonunions, and
osteomyelitis that occur after fracture. FRI may occur in the early or late postoperative
period; the latter frequently is associated with delayed fracture healing or osteomyelitis.
Acute FRI occurs within 6 weeks postoperatively, whereas chronic FRI occurs more than 6
weeks postoperatively. This distinction is largely arbitrary but may have practical
applications in terms of the pathogenesis of bacterial biofilm.1
FRI may be caused by bacteria, yeast, or fungi. The most common infecting organisms
are Staphylococcus species (methicillin-resistant S aureus and methicillin-sensitive S
aureus, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus), Enterococcus, and Pseudomonas. These

organisms may vary with regard to time of presentation (acute versus chronic) and by
season and geography.3
Biofilm-Bacteria Complex
Bacteria normally exist in a planktonic phase. After they inhabit a biofilm, they assume a more
dormant, slow metabolic rate.
The biofilm-bacteria complex is the entity comprising the bacteria in an extracellular matrix
with a glycocalyx.
This matrix is avascular, making penetration of antibiotic agents difficult.
Depending on the microbe, the biofilm layer usually forms 8 to 14 days after planktonic
colonization of the bone.
A mature biofilm complex represents the greatest barrier to management and effective
eradication of musculoskeletal infections.
Biofilm is difficult to eradicate because the slow metabolic rate impairs antibiotic effectiveness;
the biofilm impairs efficacy because it represents a barrier to diffusion.

Biofilm-Bacteria Complex
Bacteria normally exist in a planktonic phase; they are mobile, float freely, and exhibit a
high metabolic rate. After the bacteria inhabit a biofilm, they assume a more dormant,
slow metabolic rate. This altered metabolic rate may limit their antibiotic sensitivity.
Biofilm represents the first-line response of bacterial colonization, in which the initial
colony invasion sacrifices itself to create a bacteria-friendly environment for the rest of
the colony to inhabit. It consists of a dead bacterial sludge milieu.

Prolonged tourniquet use
Rough handling of soft tissues

Type of wound closure

Risk Factors
Risk factors for FRI are broadly categorized into patient factors, injury factors, and
management factors. Patients who use nicotine, have obesity, or are otherwise
immunosuppressed have an increased risk of FRI. Similarly, patients with increasing
severity of open fracture, particularly those associated with vascular injury, have an
increased risk of FRI. Various management factors, including the timing of antibiotic
administration for open fractures, the use of a staged treatment protocol, the adequacy
of initial surgical débridement, incision placement, the proximity of incisions to prior
external fixation, and the duration of surgical management, also may affect the risk of
FRI.


Definition
FRI is any infection associated with a fracture and is differentiated from prosthetic joint
infection or infection that occurs without prior fracture. Classically, terms such as deep
infection, infected nonunion, and osteomyelitis have been used to describe the entities
currently referred to as FRI.
The European Bone and Joint Infection Society, the AO Foundation, and the Orthopaedic
Trauma Association collaborated on a consensus definition of FRI, which was published
in 2018 and later updated.4 The presence of any confirmatory criterion is diagnostic for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:51 AM
AAOS | Diagnosis and Management of Fracture-Related Infection
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000534
5/24

FRI. The presence of a suggestive criterion should prompt additional investigation to
identify a confirmatory criterion.
Confirmatory criteria include the presence of a sinus tract or wound breakdown with
exposure of or communication to bone or implant, the presence of frank pus in the
surgical field or wound drainage, visible microorganisms on histopathologic examination
of samples collected during surgical management, phenotypically indistinguishable
organisms identified from two or more separate deep-tissue specimens, and more than
five polymorphonuclear lymphocytes per high-power field (×400 magnification). The last
criterion was added later and applies only to infections more than 8 weeks after fracture
based on findings that the absence of polymorphonuclear lymphocytes was associated
with aseptic nonunion.5
Suggestive criteria include a pathogen identified from a single deep-tissue specimen
(may be considered confirmatory if >50 colony forming units per mL of a virulent
organism, such as S aureus, are noted); clinical signs and symptoms of infection, such as
warmth, erythema, induration, or swelling; radiographic findings, such as peri-implant
lysis, nonunion, or sequestrum, or nuclear imaging findings; elevated serum
inflammatory markers; wound drainage beyond the first few days postoperatively; and
new-onset joint effusion in a patient with a fracture.
This definition differs from the Centers for Disease Control and Pre definition, which
includes purulent drainage, organisms isolated from fluid/tissue, at least one sign of
inflammation, and a wound that is deliberately opened by the surgeon and declared
infected.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Tissue Culture
The diagnosis of FRI depends on obtaining appropriate culture specimens.
A minimum of five tissue samples should be sent to the microbiology laboratory.
Draining wounds or sinus tracts should not be cultured preoperatively. Typically, these are
colonized and multiple or different organisms will be identified compared with deep cultures.

Laboratory Studies
A complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive
protein level are commonly ordered in the evaluation of FRI.
Monitoring these laboratory studies over time may help determine response to therapy.
The utility of biomarkers in identifying infection in patients with a nonunion is a subject of
debate.
Imaging Studies
Radiographic evaluation of the affected limb segment is performed.
Imaging is focused on assessing the maintenance of reduction, presence of nonunion, or
extent of infection for surgical planning.
Long-standing FRI may radiographically present as areas of osteolysis acutely, then as areas of
dense sclerotic bone chronically because of the avascular, necrotic nature of osteomyelitic
bone.
A necrotic segment of free, devascularized, infected bone left in a limb over time appears
radiodense on radiographs and is called a sequestrum (Figure 1). Occasionally, it is engulfed
and surrounded or walled off by healthy bone; it is then called an involucrum.

Imaging Studies
Evaluation of patients with a potential FRI should focus on establishing a diagnosis of a
FRI and providing the treating surgeon with the information necessary to create a
treatment plan.
The most critical step in establishing the diagnosis of FRI is obtaining tissue cultures. A
minimum of five tissue cultures should be sent to the microbiology laboratory. A recent
study determined that sending only three cultures results in missing 10% of FRIs.6
Ideally, each specimen should be obtained using a fresh instrument and culture tube. If

Cutibacterium acnes or unusual organisms are suspected, holding cultures for 2 weeks
may be advisable. New interest has focused on using polymerase chain reaction analysis
of specimens to determine whether microbial DNA is present and to diagnose microbial
infection.
Laboratory studies may be elevated or normal. They mostly are observed over time to
monitor a patient’s response to treatment; however, in patients with a nonunion,
elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and white blood cell
count should increase suspicion for infection. The absence of abnormal laboratory
studies does not preclude infection. An analysis of high-risk nonunions demonstrated
that, even in the absence of abnormal biomarkers, the risk of infection was 18%.7 Other
studies have suggested that these biomarkers are of little utility in patients with a
nonunion.8
Radiographs rarely are diagnostic for infection. Rather, they may provide information
about the adequacy of fracture fixation, the presence of nonunion, or the extent of
infection and necessary surgical débridement.
Types of Fracture-Related Infection
FRI is inclusive of postoperative infection, infection associated with nonunion, and
osteomyelitis.
Postoperative Infection
Superficial infection: involving only the skin and subcutaneous tissues
Deep infection: involving muscle and bone
Infected Nonunion
The presence of infection must be excluded in all patients with a nonunion.
A history of open fracture, prior infection, or absence of an obvious reason for the nonunion
should increase suspicion for infection.
Elimination of infection must occur for union to be achieved.

Types of Osteomyelitis
Acute osteomyelitis
Characterized by rapid presentation and a rapidly evident purulent infection; represents the
first episode of bone infection.
Acute osteomyelitis may become chronic over time.
Chronic osteomyelitis
Chronic osteomyelitis may be present for decades.
Chronic osteomyelitis can convert from a dormant to an active state without a known
antecedent event or from a local or systemic change in the patient.
Classification of Osteomyelitis

System for Osteomyelitis (Table 1).

Management
General Treatment Principles
Successful management of FRI can be achieved with adherence to the following principles:
Medical optimization of the patient
Radical débridement of all nonviable tissue and material
Attaining and/or maintaining skeletal stability

Delivery of local and/or systemic antibiotic agents
Ensuring a healed and viable soft-tissue envelope
Medical Management
Patient optimization
All modifiable risk factors should be addressed to maximize the likelihood of a successful
outcome. Ideally, this is done preoperatively in patients with a chronic condition but may
need to be done concurrent with management of more acute FRI.
Nicotine cessation likely is the most important step to improve the likelihood of successful
management of infection.
Optimization of a patient’s nutritional status via an assessment of albumin and prealbumin
levels and via dietary supplementation as necessary
Improving glycemic control for patients with diabetes mellitus
Delivery of systemic antibiotic agents
Parenteral antibiotic agents are administered after débridement and are tailored to
sensitivities from intraoperative cultures.
Treatment protocols frequently involve a 6-week intravenous antibiotic regimen.
With the sharp increase in organisms developing antibiotic resistance (such as methicillin-
resistant S aureus and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), an appropriate antibiotic regimen
may need to include daptomycin.
In certain patients (type C patients), long-term antibiotic suppression may be the preferred
treatment option.
Surgical Management
Surgical débridement
Surgical débridement is the cornerstone of the management of FRI (Video 1).
Adequate débridement is achieved after all infected and devitalized bone and tissue have
been excised.
Débridement of any dense fibrotic scarring also is necessary because it often is avascular
and represents a poor soft-tissue bed for healing.
Atrophic skin that has become adherent to the bone (eg, the medial border of the tibia) also
requires débridement because of its impaired blood supply and compliance.

Skeletal stabilization
For recently fixed fractures, maintenance of skeletal stability via implant retention is
preferred and likely to be successful.
For longer-standing FRI, such as in nonunions, skeletal stabilization of the affected limb is
necessary if mechanical instability results from débridement.
Stabilization is most often accomplished via external fixation. It also can be accomplished via
antibiotic-impregnated, cement-coated medullary nails or plates.
For small defects (<2 cm), acute shortening remains a reasonable treatment option,
especially in the upper extremity.
Delayed bone grafting or osteomyocutaneous free-tissue transfer also is possible after
infection eradication.
For some large osseous defects, treatment options include bone grafting with the induced
membrane technique, bone transport with distraction osteogenesis, or vascularized free

Delivery of local antibiotic agents
Antibiotic-impregnated polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) beads are useful for managing
dead space; they also provide an effective means of local, high-dose antibiotic delivery
(Figure 3).

antibiotic-loaded polymethyl methacrylate in orthopaedic practice. A, Antibiotic-loaded
polymethyl methacrylate beads alone are used for the management of an infected total knee

Most surgeons make their own beads by mixing PMMA with tobramycin and vancomycin
powder.
Other antibiotic agents used include gentamycin, erythromycin, tetracycline, and colistin. In
general, heat-stable antibiotic agents can be used.
Resorbable materials, including calcium sulfate, calcium phosphate, and hydroxyapatite
ceramic beads with antibiotic impregnation, recently have been introduced; however, their
clinical efficacy has not yet been well established.
Antibiotic-impregnated PMMA beads can be effectively used with or without a closed soft-
tissue envelope.
With an open soft-tissue envelope, the beads can be placed, and the limb and wound are
then wrapped with an adhesive-coated plastic film laminate. This provides a biologic barrier
with high-dose local antibiotic agent delivery and usually works well for 4 to 6 days before
changing is required because of leakage.
With a closed soft-tissue envelope, the beads can be left in place for an extended period to
ensure that infection has been controlled.
Antibiotic beads should not be placed beneath negative-pressure wound dressings unless
they are beneath a tightly closed fascia because this will pull away the antibiotic agent and
reduce levels below the minimum inhibitory concentration.
PMMA also can be used to coat medullary nails and/or plates (Figure 4).

Various tubes (eg, chest tube, perfusion tube) can be used as a mold for an antibiotic nail.
The inner diameter of the tube must be known to allow for reaming to create appropriate
medullary space for insertion.
The use of a standard locked nail may provide adequate stability for healing of the fracture
while eradicating the infection.
Antibiotic plates are useful in short segments and may obviate the need for joint-spanning
external fixation.
Locking towers may be used.
Ensuring a healed and viable soft-tissue envelope
If the amount of nonviable tissue débrided does not allow for safe, tension-free wound
closure, then other soft-tissue coverage options must be explored.
A close working relationship with a microsurgeon who has experience in soft-tissue
mobilization and free-tissue transfer is imperative in managing FRIs in patients with a soft-
tissue void or an impaired soft-tissue envelope.
Soft-tissue coverage options include local muscle mobilization, a rotational muscle flap, a
free muscle flap, a free fasciocutaneous flap, or a rotational perforator-based flap (Videos 5
and 6).
Rotational flaps are a good adjuvant for certain soft-tissue defects or if a microsurgeon is
not available.
Negative-pressure wound therapy is a useful short-term adjunct to aid in dead-space
management and create a sealed environment until definitive soft-tissue coverage is
achieved.
If placed directly over cortical bone for an extended period, negative-pressure wound
therapy may result in desiccation and death of the cortical bone.

Special issues in the management of infected nonunions
Endocrinologic evaluation (25-hydroxyvitamin D, thyroid-stimulating hormone, parathyroid
hormone, testosterone) should be considered in all patients with a nonunion, especially in
those with a recalcitrant nonunion.
Extra attention must be given to identifying and correcting skeletal deformity, including in
the axial plane (length and rotation).
Biologic augmentation may be necessary; typically, infection eradication should be
performed before the placement of autograft or other materials that may provide a
favorable environment for bacteria.
The treatment principles for FRI broadly apply to most nonunions; however, with nonunions,
the affected limb will have experienced trauma, surgeries, and disuse atrophy, and the
periarticular regions are prone to stiffness.
Restoration or preservation of motion via manipulation or release of surrounding joints is
essential.

Surgical Management
Successful management of FRI can be achieved by adhering to the following principles:
medical optimization of the patient, radical débridement of all nonviable tissue and
material, obtaining and/or maintaining skeletal stability, delivering local and/or systemic
antibiotic agents, and ensuring a healed and viable soft-tissue envelope.
Management of FRI begins preoperatively by making a problem list. All factors that affect
management are listed (eg, obesity, nicotine use, infected nonunion, bone defect, 2 cm
of shortening, and 20° of varus angulation); each item is addressed to the extent
possible.
Medical optimization should begin preoperatively, especially for patients with chronic or
long-standing conditions. Examples of medical optimization include nicotine cessation,
glycemic control in patients with diabetes mellitus, nutritional optimization, and
addressing other medical conditions (eg, achieving euthyroid function in patients with
hypothyroidism or increasing cluster of differentiation 4+ counts in patients with HIV). A
thorough assessment of nutritional status should be performed, including serum

identify problems and offer nutritional supplementation via protein shakes or other
methods. Many patient factors that affect management may not be modifiable (eg,
obesity, cancer); however, the emphasis of the first step of management should be
optimizing the patient.
Surgical management often requires multiple steps, depending on the nature of the FRI.
A postoperative FRI may be successfully managed via single débridement, implant
retention, and postoperative antibiotic agents. Other FRIs, such as infected nonunions,
often require multiple surgical débridement procedures followed by soft-tissue
coverage, antibiotic therapy, and osseous reconstruction.
The critical first step in the management of any infection is thorough and systematic
surgical débridement. All nonviable tissue and material should be removed, including
avascular skin or scarring, dead muscle or bone, suture material or other foreign bodies,
and surgical implants if possible. Multiple débridement procedures may be necessary
over several days to fully evaluate the extent of the infection and adequately débride the
area.
Skeletal stability is essential for any FRI.9 Simple splint immobilization may reduce shear
through the soft tissues and expedite recovery. In patients with an early postoperative
FRI and a well-reduced and fixed fracture, maintenance of the implants is beneficial if
possible. This strategy is effective less than 10 weeks postoperatively.5 In other patients,
complete implant removal is warranted. Skeletal stability may be achieved with the use
of uniplanar or ringed external fixators or PMMA-coated antibiotic medullary nails or
plates.10,11
Local antibiotic agents may be delivered via various methods. Antibiotic-coated
medullary nails or plates will provide local antibiotic delivery to the medullary canal or
periarticular region. Similarly, PMMA can be impregnated with any heat-stable antibiotic
or antifungal agent and molded into beads that can be placed into dead space in the
wound. Dissolvable antibiotic delivery methods, such as calcium sulfate pellets that are
mixed with antibiotics, have been described; however, evidence on their effectiveness is
lacking (Video 7).

Lastly, a viable soft-tissue envelope is necessary for infection eradication and limb
function. In many patients, resection of relatively avascular scarring or questionably
viable tissue and subsequent soft-tissue transfer is preferable to maintaining a tenuous
soft-tissue envelope. Muscle flaps are associated with good blood flow that can bring
parenteral antibiotic agents to the necessary region. Various rotational soft-tissue flaps
are well described and within the knowledge and skill set of orthopaedic surgeons;
however, surgeons who commonly manage FRIs require a strong relationship with a
reconstructive plastic surgeon because free-tissue transfer often is necessary. The use of
muscular or fasciocutaneous flaps are well described, and flap selection often depends
on patient or injury-specific factors.
